name: Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Causes slowly progressive, asymmetrical, distal, upper-limb-predominant weakness in the distribution of individual nerves
Sensation is characteristically preserved, an important feature separating it from other polyneuropathies
The electrophysiological hallmark is motor conduction block at sites not prone to compression, with normal sensory conduction across the same segments
Serum anti-GM1 ganglioside antibodies are positive in a substantial proportion and support the diagnosis
It is often mistaken for motor neuron disease, but the pure motor picture is potentially treatable
Intravenous immunoglobulin is the mainstay of treatment, whereas corticosteroids and plasma exchange are typically unhelpful or may worsen the condition
Cerebrospinal fluid protein is usually normal or only mildly raised, unlike CIDP
reference.pathophysiology: Multifocal motor neuropathy is an immune-mediated disorder of motor axons in which antibodies, frequently against the GM1 ganglioside enriched at the node of Ranvier, disrupt nodal sodium-channel clusters and paranodal architecture. This produces persistent focal conduction block along motor fibres while sensory fibres are spared, generating the pattern of weakness confined to individual nerve territories without sensory loss. Over time some axonal degeneration occurs, but the primary and treatment-responsive abnormality is the focal motor conduction block, which explains both the clinical picture and the benefit from immunoglobulin therapy.
additionalDifferentials: Motor neuron disease (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, progressive muscular atrophy)
Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies to demonstrate motor conduction block with preserved sensory conduction
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis to help distinguish from CIDP
MRI or ultrasound of nerves and plexus to show focal enlargement or signal change
Electromyography to assess for denervation and exclude anterior horn cell disease
Assessment of treatment response to intravenous immunoglobulin as supportive evidence
redFlags: Emerging upper motor neuron signs suggesting motor neuron disease rather than MMN
Development of sensory involvement prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Rapid axonal loss with wasting threatening irreversible weakness
Loss of previously good response to immunoglobulin therapy
reference.prognosis: Many patients maintain function with regular intravenous immunoglobulin, though the disorder is usually chronic and requires ongoing treatment; progressive axonal loss can cause slowly accumulating disability over years.
pitfalls: Diagnosing motor neuron disease and missing a treatable neuropathy
Treating with corticosteroids or plasma exchange, which may be ineffective or harmful
Excluding the diagnosis when anti-GM1 antibodies are negative
Failing to search adequately for conduction block outside common entrapment sites
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Intravenous immunoglobulin as first-line and maintenance therapy, with subcutaneous immunoglobulin as an alternative for maintenance
Immunosuppressants such as cyclophosphamide or rituximab reserved for immunoglobulin-refractory disease
Avoid corticosteroids and plasma exchange, which are typically ineffective and may worsen the condition
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and orthotic support to maintain function
Regular assessment of strength, disability and treatment response to titrate the immunoglobulin dosing interval
Neuromuscular specialist management that distinguishes the disorder from motor neuron disease so that treatable disease is not missed
